USE OF CERTAIN MEDICINES. Taking penicillins with certain other drugs may affect the way the drugs work or may increase the chance of side effects.

Context: This section provides examples of specific penicillin medications, including their brand names and formulations, as well as warnings about potential side effects related to sodium content in low-sodium diets. It serves as a reference guide for understanding the different types of penicillins available.

Content: Examples of penicillins are penicillin V (Beepen-VK, Pen-Vee K, V-cillin K, Veetids) and amoxicillin (Amoxil, Polymox, Trimox, Wymox). Penicillins are sometimes combined with other ingredients called beta-lactamase inhibitors, which protect the penicillin from bacterial enzymes that may destroy it before it can do its work. The drug Augmentin, for example, contains a combination of amoxicillin and a betalactamase inhibitor, clavulanic acid.  
LOW-SODIUM DIET. Some penicillin medicines contain large enough amounts of sodium to cause problems for people on low-sodium diets. Anyone on such a diet should make sure that the physician treating the infection knows about the special diet.

Context: This chunk describes common side effects that are generally mild, resolving on their own as the body adjusts to the medication, unless they persist or cause discomfort. In contrast to other sections discussing more severe and potentially life-threatening side effects, this section highlights the relatively minor issues often associated with opioid analgesics.

Content: The most common side effects are mild diarrhea, headache, vaginal itching and discharge, sore mouth or tongue, or white patches in the mouth or on the tongue. These problems usually go away as the body adjusts to the drug and do not require medical treatment unless they continue or they are bothersome.
More serious side effects are not common, but may occur. If any of the following side effects occur, get emergency medical help immediately:
- breathing problems, such as shortness of breath or fast or irregular breathing
- fever
- sudden lightheadedness or faintness  ## Interactions

Context: Interaction with other medications, particularly antibiotics like penicillin, may alter their effects or increase side effect risk. Individuals taking penicillin should inform their physician about all concurrent medications, as interactions can occur with various prescription and over-the-counter drugs that relieve pain, treat hormonal imbalances, and thin blood.

Content: Birth control pills may not work properly when taken at the same time as penicillin. To prevent pregnancy, use additional methods of birth control while taking penicillin, such as latex condoms or spermicide.
Penicillins may interact with many other medicines. When this happens, the effects of one or both of the drugs may change or the risk of side effects may be greater. Anyone who takes penicillin should let the physician know all other medicines he or she is taking. Among the drugs that may interact with penicillins are:
- Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and other medicines that relieve pain and inflammation
- medicine for overactive thyroid
- male hormones (androgens)
- female hormones (estrogens)
- other antibiotics
- blood thinners

Context: This section discusses medications that may interact with penicillins, highlighting potential risks of adverse interactions when combined. It provides guidance on seeking medical advice before taking certain prescription or nonprescription medicines alongside penicillins, ensuring safe use and minimizing side effects.

Content: - Disulfiram (Antabuse), used to treat alcohol abuse
- antiseizure medicines such as Depakote and Depakene
- blood pressure drugs such as Capoten, Monopril, and Lotensin
The list above does not include every drug that may interact with penicillins. Be sure to check with a physician or pharmacist before combining penicillins with any other prescription or nonprescription (overthe-counter) medicine.

Context: This section appears unrelated to side effects, as it discusses terms such as enzyme, microorganism, mononucleosis, and Nancy Ross-Flanigan, which do not fit within the scope of the "Side effects" topic.

Content: Enzyme—A type of protein that brings about or speeds up chemical reactions.
Microorganism—An organism that is too small to be seen with the naked eye.
Mononucleosis—An infectious disease with symptoms that include severe fatigue, fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes in the neck and armpits. Also called ''mono.''
Nancy Ross-Flanigan

Context: Definition of penile cancer, describing it as the growth of malignant cells on the external skin and in the tissues of the penis, serving as a foundational concept to understand the disease's characteristics.

Content: Penile cancer is the growth of malignant cells on the external skin and in the tissues of the penis.

Context: This chunk discusses the initial definition and progression of penile cancer, explaining how cancerous cells can develop on the penis if left untreated, leading to potential spread to lymph nodes and other parts of the body.

Content: Penile cancer is a disease in which cancerous cells appear on the penis. If left untreated, this cancer can grow and spread from the penis to the lymph nodes in the groin and eventually to other parts of the body.

Context: This information provides an overview of the prevalence of penile cancer globally, highlighting its rarity in the US and relative frequency in Africa and Asia.

Content: Penile cancer is a rare form of cancer that develops in about one out of 100,000 men per year in the United States. Penile cancer is more common in other parts of the world, particularly Africa and Asia. In Uganda, penile cancer is the most common form of cancer for men.

Context: In Penile cancer, understanding the cause and symptoms is crucial. The most common symptoms of penile cancer are described here, including a tender spot or open sore, unusual liquid discharges, and pain or bleeding in the genital area, which may indicate the onset of this rare but potentially life-threatening form of cancer.

Content: The cause of penile cancer is unknown. The most common symptoms of penile cancer are:  
- a tender spot, an open sore, or a wart-like lump on the penis
- unusual liquid discharges from the penis
- pain or bleeding in the genital area

Context: In order to diagnose penile cancer, medical professionals perform an examination and potentially order a biopsy to confirm the presence of cancerous cells, distinguishing it from other conditions such as syphilis or warts. This diagnostic process is a crucial step in determining the stage and treatment options for penile cancer.

Content: In order to diagnose penile cancer, the doctor examines the patient's penis for lumps or other abnormalities. A tissue sample, or biopsy, may be ordered to distinguish cancerous cells from syphilis and penile warts. If the results confirm a diagnosis of cancer, additional tests are done to determine whether the disease has spread to other parts of the body.

Context: This section provides detailed information on treatment options for penile cancer, specifically focusing on stages I, II, III, and IV, including surgical procedures, medical treatments such as microsurgery and fluorouracil cream, and radiation therapy. It outlines various treatment approaches to manage the disease at different stages of progression.

Content: In Stage I penile cancer, malignant cells are found only on the surface of the head (glans) and on the foreskin of the penis. If the cancer is limited to the foreskin, treatment may involve wide local excision and circumcision. Wide local excision is a form of surgery that removes only cancer cells and a small amount of normal tissue adjacent to them. Circumcision is removal of the foreskin.
If the Stage I cancer is only on the glans, treatment may involve the use of a fluorouracil cream (Adrucil, Efudex), and/or microsurgery. Microsurgery removes cancerous tissue and the smallest possible amount of normal tissue. During microsurgery, the doctor uses a special instrument that provides a comprehensive view of the area where cancer cells are located and makes it possible to determine that all malignant cells have been removed.
In Stage II, the penile cancer has spread to the surface of the glans, tissues beneath the surface, and the shaft of the penis. The treatment recommended may be amputation of all or part of the penis (total or partial penectomy). If the disease is diagnosed early enough, surgeons are often able to preserve enough of the organ for urination and sexual activity. Treatment may also include microsurgery and external radiation therapy, in which a machine provides radiation to the affected area. Laser surgery is an experimental treatment for Stage II cancers. Laser surgery uses an intense precisely focused beam of light to dissolve or burn away cancer cells.
In Stage III, malignant cells have spread to lymph nodes in the groin, where they cause swelling. The recommended treatment may include amputation of the penis and removal of the lymph nodes on both sides. Radiation therapy may also be suggested. More advanced disease requires systemic treatments using drugs (chemotherapy). In chemotherapy, medicines are administered intravenously or taken by mouth. These drugs enter the bloodstream and kill cancer cells that have spread to any part of the body.
In Stage IV, the disease has spread throughout the penis and lymph nodes in the groin, or has traveled to other parts of the body. Treatments are similar to that for Stage III cancer.

Context: Recurrent penile cancer is discussed in relation to the prognosis and treatment outcomes of the disease, highlighting that while cure rates are generally high for early-stage cancers, recurrence rates increase for more advanced stages where cancer cells have spread to lymph nodes.

Content: Recurrent penile cancer is disease that recurs in the penis or develops in another part of the body after treatment has eradicated the original cancer cells.  Cure rates are high for cancers diagnosed in Stage I or II, but much lower for Stages III and IV, by which time cancer cells have spread to the lymph nodes.

Context: "Treatments for penile cancer, including surgical procedures such as circumcision and topical medications like fluorouracil, are discussed in detail."

Content: Circumcision—Surgical removal of the foreskin of the penis. It is usually performed shortly after birth.  
Fluorouracil—A cell-killing (cytotoxic) medication that can be applied in cream form to treat cancer of the penis.

Context: Biological therapy is an experimental treatment approach being studied as part of penile cancer treatment, focusing on boosting the body's immune response to combat cancer cells. This innovative method aims to reinforce the body's disease-fighting resources using natural or artificial substances.

Content: In addition to the treatments previously described, biological therapy is another treatment that is currently being studied. Biological therapy is a type of treatment that is sometimes called biological response modifier (BRM) therapy. It uses natural or artificial substances to boost, focus, or reinforce the body's disease-fighting resources.

Context: This section lists conditions that increase a person's risk of developing penile cancer, including infections, skin diseases, and other factors that cause repeated irritation to the penis. It is relevant to understanding the causes and risk factors associated with penile cancer, providing insight into the potential triggers for the disease.

Content: Conditions which increase a person's chance of getting penile cancer include:
- infection with genital warts (human papillomavirus, or HPV)
- a skin disease called psoriasis

Context: Risk factors for penile cancer include various medical conditions, lifestyle habits, and personal hygiene practices. Conditions like phimosis, skin diseases, and smoking increase the risk, as do poor cleansing habits and being uncircumcised, highlighting the importance of preventive measures in reducing the likelihood of developing this rare form of cancer.

Content: - a condition called phimosis, in which the foreskin becomes difficult to retract
- other conditions that result in repeated irritation of the penis.
- a history of smoking.
There appears to be a connection between development of the disease and lack of personal hygiene. Failure to regularly and thoroughly cleanse the part of the penis covered by the foreskin increases the risk of developing the disease. Penile cancer is also more common in uncircumcised men.

Context: This chunk explains the basic purpose and function of penile prostheses, specifically their role in alleviating impotence by providing a mechanical solution to maintain an erection.

Content: Penile prostheses are semirigid or inflatable devices that are implanted into penises to alleviate impotence.

Context: An overview of penile prosthesis function, anatomy, and potential causes of impotence, explaining how these factors relate to the implantation procedure and its benefits in alleviating erectile dysfunction.

Content: The penis is composed of one channel for urine and semen and three compartments with tough, fibrous walls containing ''erectile tissue.'' With appropriate stimulation, the blood vessels that lead out of these compartments constrict, trapping blood. Blood pressure fills and hardens the compartments producing an erection of sufficient firmness to perform sexual intercourse. Additional stimulation leads to ejaculation, where semen is pumped out of the urethra. When this system fails, impotence (failure to create and maintain an erection) occurs.  
Impotence can be caused by a number of conditions, including diabetes, spinal cord injury, prolonged drug abuse, and removal of a prostate gland. If the medical condition is irreversible, a penile prosthesis may be considered. Patients whose impotence is caused by psychological problems are not recommended for implant surgery.

Context: This excerpt describes the surgical procedure of penile implant surgery, detailing the types of devices used (semirigid vs. inflatable), the process of implantation, and the post-operative care required for patients undergoing this treatment to alleviate impotence.

Content: Penile implant surgery is conducted on patients who have exhausted all other areas of treatment. The semirigid device consists of two rods that are easier and less expensive to implant than the inflatable cylinders. Once implanted, the semirigid device needs no follow-up adjustments, however it produces a penis which constantly remains semi-erect. The inflatable cylinders produce a more natural effect. The patient is able to simulate an erection by using a pump located in the scrotum.  
With the patient asleep under general anesthesia, the device is inserted into the erectile tissue of the penis through an incision in the fibrous wall. In order to implant the pump for the inflatable implant, incisions are made in the abdomen and the perineum (area between the anus and the genitals). A fluid reservoir is inserted into the groin and the pump is placed in the scrotum. The cylinders, reservoir, and pump are connected by tubes and tested before the incisions are closed.

Context: This section provides essential information on the preparation and informed consent process for penile prosthesis surgery, emphasizing the importance of a well-informed patient and their sexual partner. It also outlines the necessary pre-surgical procedures, including antibacterial cleansing and shaving, to minimize risks and ensure a successful outcome.

Content: Surgery always requires an adequately informed patient, both as to risks and benefits. In this case, the sexual partner should also be involved in the discussion. Prior to surgery, antibacterial cleansing occurs and the surrounding areas are shaved.

Context: This section provides definitions related to medical terminology used in penile prosthesis surgery, including key terms like general anesthesia, genital areas, perineum, and scrotum, providing essential background information for understanding the surgical procedure.

Content: General anesthesia—Deep sleep induced by a combination of medicines that allows surgery to be performed.  
Genital—Sexual organ.  
Perineum—Area between the anus and genitals.  
Scrotum—The external pouch containing the male reproductive glands (testes) and part of the spermatic cord.

Context: Following penile implant surgery, patients need to manage post-operative care, including preventing swelling, infection, and pain. This includes applying ice packs and performing daily cleansing, as well as taking pain relievers and monitoring for potential risks associated with the new device, such as infection and irritation.

Content: To minimize swelling, ice packs are applied to the penis for the first 24 hours following surgery. The incision sites are cleansed daily to prevent infection. Pain relievers may be taken.  ## Risks
With any implant, there is a slightly greater risk of infection. The implant may irritate the penis and cause continuous pain. The inflatable prosthesis may need follow-up surgery to repair leaks in the reservoir or to reconnect the tubing.

Context: This sentence introduces Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC) as a diagnostic test used to identify obstructions in the liver or bile ducts, explaining its purpose in relation to the flow of bile from the liver to the digestive system.

Content: Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTHC) is an x-ray test used to identify obstructions either in the liver or bile ducts that slow or stop the flow of bile from the liver to the digestive system.

Context: This chunk describes how the liver is prepared for Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC) by injecting a special dye to visualize the bile ducts, which helps identify obstructions or blockages that may be causing symptoms.

Content: Because the liver and bile ducts are not normally seen on x rays, the doctor injects the liver with a special dye that will show up on the resulting picture. This dye distributes evenly to fill the whole liver drainage system. If the dye does not distribute evenly, this is indicative of a blockage, which may be caused by a gallstone or a tumor in the liver, bile ducts, or pancreas.

Context: Patients with certain medical conditions are not ideal candidates for PTHC, as they may be at risk of complications. This warning advises individuals with specific health concerns, including cholangitis, ascites, severe iodine allergies, or bleeding disorders, to inform their doctor before undergoing the procedure, while also emphasizing the importance of disclosing diabetes status.

Content: PTHC should not be performed on anyone who has cholangitis (inflammation of the bile duct), massive ascites, a severe allergy to iodine, or a serious uncorrectable or uncontrollable bleeding disorder. Patients who have diabetes should inform their doctor.

Context: Patients undergoing Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC) should be aware of potential allergic reactions to various substances, including anesthetics, dyes used in medical tests, iodine, and shellfish, which may impact test safety and outcomes. This information is crucial for patients to report any such reactions to their healthcare provider before the procedure.

Content: Patients should report allergic reactions to:
- anesthetics
- dyes used in medical tests
- iodine
- shellfish

Context: This chunk describes the procedure and steps involved in performing Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC), a medical imaging test used to visualize the bile ducts, outlining the equipment, preparation, and patient experience during the procedure.

Content: PTHC is performed in a hospital, doctor's office, or outpatient surgical or x-ray facility. The patient lies on a movable x-ray table and is given a local anesthetic. The patient will be told to hold his or her breath, and a doctor, nurse, or laboratory technician will inject a special dye into the liver as the patient exhales.
The patient may feel a twinge when the needle penetrates the liver, a pressure or fullness, or brief discomfort in the upper right side of the back. Hands and feet may become numb during the 30–60 minute procedure.
The x-ray table will be rotated several times during the test, and the patient helped to assume a variety of positions. A special x-ray machine called a fluoroscope will track the dye's movement through the bile ducts and show whether the fluid is moving freely or if its passage is obstructed.
PTHC costs about \$1,600. The test may have to be repeated if the patient moves while x rays are being taken.

Context: To aid in identifying potential complications related to Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC), patients may be prescribed an intravenous antibiotic, advised to fast overnight, and asked to discontinue certain medications before undergoing the procedure. This section of information highlights crucial pre-test preparations for PTHC.

Content: An intravenous antibiotic may be given every 4–6 hours during the 24 hours before the test. The patient will be told to fast overnight. Having an empty stomach is a safety measure in case of complications, such as bleeding, that might require emergency repair surgery. Medications such as aspirin, or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that thin the blood, should be stopped three–seven days prior to taking the PRHC test. Patients may also be given a sedative a few minutes before the test begins.

Context: Following an invasive procedure, patients undergoing Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC) require specific post-procedure care to minimize complications. This includes rest, eating habits adjustments, and timely monitoring for potential adverse reactions or infections.

Content: The patient should stay in bed for at least six hours after the test, lying on the right side to prevent bleeding from the injection site. The patient may resume normal eating habits and gradually resume normal activities. The doctor should be informed right away if pain develops in the right abdomen or shoulder or in case of fever, dizziness, or a change in stool color to black or red.

Context: A nurse's vital sign monitoring during Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC) is crucial to detect potential complications, such as allergic reactions or signs of infection, allowing timely intervention and preventing serious consequences like septicemia or bile peritonitis. This monitoring helps ensure patient safety throughout the procedure.

Content: A nurse will monitor the patient's vital signs and watch for:
- itching
- flushing
- nausea and vomiting
- sweating
- excessive flow of saliva
- possible serious allergic reactions to contrast dye

Context: This section highlights two serious, although rare, potential complications of Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC), a medical imaging procedure used to diagnose blockages in liver and bile ducts. These complications include septicemia and bile peritonitis, emphasizing the importance of careful patient monitoring during the test.

Content: Septicemia (blood poisoning) and bile peritonitis (a potentially fatal infection or inflammation of the membrane covering the walls of the abdomen) are rare but serious complications of this procedure. Dye occasionally leaks from the liver into the abdomen, and there is a slight risk of bleeding or infection.

Context: This statement explains how normal results appear on an x-ray during PTHC, highlighting potential factors that may affect test outcomes, such as obesity or failure to fast.

Content: Normal x rays show dye evenly distributed throughout the bile ducts. Obesity, gas, and failure to fast can affect test results.

Context: This section outlines possible causes of enlarged bile ducts, which may indicate various conditions such as liver disease, gallstones, or cancers. The information is relevant to Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC), a diagnostic test used to visualize the bile ducts and identify potential obstructions or abnormalities.

Content: Enlargement of bile ducts may indicate:  
- obstructive or non-obstructive jaundice
- cholelithiasis (gallstones)
- hepatitis (inflammation of the liver)
- cirrhosis (chronic liver disease)
- granulomatous disease
- pancreatic cancer
- bile duct or gallbladder cancers

Context: The provided text defines key characteristics and consequences of a perforated eardrum, including its definition, causes, symptoms, diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, and treatment options. This section sets the stage for understanding the condition, its effects on hearing and ear health, and ways to manage or prevent it.

Content: A perforated eardrum exists when there is a hole or rupture in the eardrum, the thin membrane that separates the outer ear canal from the middle ear. A perforated eardrum may cause temporary hearing loss and occasional discharge.

Context: This section provides definitions and explanations related to key medical terms, specifically those relevant to Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC), including Ascites, Bile Ducts, Cholangitis, and Fluoroscope. These terms are crucial for understanding the procedure's context, risks, and potential complications, making them essential knowledge for patients undergoing PTHC.

Content: Ascites—Abnormal accumulation of fluid in the abdomen.
Bile ducts—Tubes that carry bile, a thick yellowishgreen fluid that is made by the liver, stored in the gallbladder, and helps the body digest fats.
Cholangitis—Inflammation of the bile duct.
Fluoroscope—An x-ray machine that projects images of organs.

Context: This section describes two medical conditions that may be related to bile duct issues, including jaundice caused by obstructive or non-obstructive problems in the liver. These conditions, along with granulomatous disease, are potential causes of abnormal findings during a Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTHC) test, which aims to diagnose obstructions in the liver and bile ducts.

Content: Granulomatous disease—Characterized by growth of tiny blood vessels and connective tissue.
Jaundice—Disease that causes bile to accumulate in the blood, causing the skin and whites of the eyes to turn yellow. Obstructive jaundice is caused by blockage of bile ducts, while non-obstructive jaundice is caused by disease or infection of the liver.

Context: This chunk provides detailed information about the structure, function, and impact of a perforated eardrum on hearing, including how it causes temporary hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear infections.

Content: The eardrum (tympanic membrane) is a thin wall that separates the outer ear from the middle ear, vibrating when sound waves strike the membrane. The middle ear is connected to the nose by the Eustachian tube.  
In addition to conducting sound, the eardrum also protects the middle ear from bacteria. When it is perforated, bacteria can more easily get into this part of the ear, causing ear infections.  
In general, the larger the hole in the eardrum, the greater the temporary loss of hearing. The location of the perforation also affects the degree of hearing loss. Severe hearing loss may follow a skull fracture that disrupts the bones in the middle ear. Eardrum perforation caused by a loud noise may result in ringing in the ear (tinnitus), in addition to a temporary hearing loss. Over time, this hearing loss improves and the ringing usually fades in a few days.

Context: This section discusses various causes of an ear drum perforation, including sudden traumatic injuries such as skull fractures or loud noises, as well as complications from infections. It explains how these conditions can lead to eardrum damage, symptoms, diagnosis, and treatment, providing a comprehensive overview of the topic.

Content: - after a skull fracture
- after a loud explosion or other loud noise
In addition, an ear infection can rupture the eardrum as pressure within the middle ear rises when fluid builds up. If the eardrum is punctured by pressure from an ear infection, there may be infected or bloody drainage from the ear.
Rarely, a small hole may remain in the eardrum after a pressure-equalizing tube falls out or is removed by a doctor.
Symptoms include an earache or pain in the ear, which may be severe, or a sudden decrease in ear pain, followed by ear drainage of clear, bloody, or pus-filled fluid, hearing loss, or ear noise/buzzing.

Context: A perforated eardrum can be caused by direct injury, such as using a cotton-tipped swab or hitting the ear with an open hand. This section provides examples of how a person's carelessness or accident can lead to damage to the eardrum, resulting in a hole or rupture that may cause temporary hearing loss and other symptoms.

Content: The eardrum can become damaged by a direct injury. It is possible to perforate the eardrum:
- with a cotton-tipped swab or another foreign object
- by hitting the ear with an open hand

Context: Diagnosis is an essential step in addressing a perforated eardrum, where medical professionals use otoscopes to visually inspect the eardrum and hearing tests to determine the extent of any hearing loss. This diagnostic process helps identify the condition's severity and guides treatment decisions.

Content: A doctor can diagnose a perforated eardrum by direct inspection with an otoscope. Hearing tests may reveal a hearing loss.

Context: This section discusses the prognosis and treatment outcome for a perforated eardrum, outlining its general healing process, temporary hearing loss, and potential need for antibiotics. It provides reassurance on the condition's self-healing nature and temporary symptoms, setting the stage for further discussions on prevention measures and management strategies.

Content: A perforated eardrum usually heals by itself within two months. Antibiotics may be given to  ## Prognosis
While a perforated eardrum may be uncomfortable, it usually heals on its own. Any hearing loss that accompanies the perforation is usually temporary.

Context: This chunk defines the condition, highlighting its specific location within the nose's anatomy. It sets the stage for explaining the causes and treatment options of a perforated septum, providing an overview of the condition's nature.

Content: A perforated septum is a hole in the nasal septum, the vertical plane of tissue that separates the nostrils.

Context: This section provides contact information, definitions, and explanation of medical equipment related to otolaryngology (ear, nose, and throat) specialties and procedures, which is relevant to understanding the diagnosis, treatment, and management of a perforated eardrum.

Content: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, Inc. One Prince St., Alexandria VA 22314- 3357. (703) 836-4444. <http://www.entnet.org>. Better Hearing Institute. 515 King Street, Suite 420, Alexandria, VA 22314. (703) 684-3391.  
Eustachian tube—The air duct that connects the area behind the nose to the middle ear.  
Otoscope—An instrument used to examine the ear, to inspect the outer ear canal and the eardrum, and to detect diseases in the middle ear.

Context: Preventing perforation of the eardrum involves avoiding self-insertion or manipulation, seeking medical attention if a foreign object is lodged in the ear, and promptly treating all ear infections to avoid rupturing the eardrum. Proper prevention measures can help reduce the risk of complications associated with perforated eardrums.

Content: A perforated eardrum can be prevented by avoiding insertion of any object into the ear to clean it. If a foreign object becomes lodged in the ear, only a doctor should try to remove it.  
Promptly treating all ear infections is another way to guard against a ruptured eardrum.

Context: This chunk describes the structure and function of the nasal septum, explaining how its blood supply can be disrupted, leading to a perforation. It provides essential background information on the anatomy and physiology of the nasal septum, making it relevant to understanding the causes and implications of a perforated septum.

Content: The nasal septum is a thin structure in the middle of the nose. In front, it is cartilage, further back it is bone. On either side, it is covered with mucus membranes. The cartilage depends upon the blood vessels in the mucus membranes on either side for its nutrition. If that blood supply is shut off, the cartilage dies, producing a hole or perforation.

Context: This section discusses common causes of a perforated septum, including nasal ornament use and cocaine sniffing, which can damage blood vessels leading to cartilage death and subsequent hole formation.

Content: There are several causes of a perforated septum.
- Wearing ornaments in the nose. To hang an ornament from the middle of the nose requires that the tissue directly in front of the septal cartilage be pierced or perforated.
- Sniffing cocaine. Cocaine is a potent vasoconstrictor, which means that it causes small blood vessels to  ## Treatment
Surgical repair is not difficult. The surgeon may devise a plastic button that fits exactly into the defect and stays in place like a collar button.

Context: Treatment options for perforated septum, including non-surgical methods such as saline nasal sprays that can help control symptoms and prevent surgery.

Content: Saline nasal sprays may be sufficient to control symptoms and prevent the need for surgery.

Context: This section discusses common treatment options for a perforated septum, specifically focusing on methods to control nosebleeds, which are a potential complication of this condition.

Content: Nosebleeds from the septum can usually be controlled with pinching. Vaginal estrogen cream has also been used successfully to toughen the blood vessels.

Context: This section discusses Systemic lupus erythematosus as a cause of perforated septum, specifically highlighting its role in causing damage to various parts of the body. It links this autoimmune condition to the underlying pathophysiology of a perforated septum, providing a connection between the broader topic of perforated septums and specific medical conditions that can lead to this issue.

Content: Systemic lupus erythematosus—A collagen-vascular disease in the autoimmune category that causes damage to many different parts of the body.

Context: This section discusses the diagnosis and management of pericarditis, a condition characterized by an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the sac surrounding the heart. It highlights the role of pericardiocentesis as both a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure to identify and remove excess fluid that may be impeding the heart's pumping action.

Content: Possible causes of pericarditis include chest trauma, systemic infection (bacterial, viral, or fungal), myocardial infarction (heart attack), or tuberculosis. When pericarditis is suspected, pericardiocentesis may be advisable in order to obtain a fluid sample for laboratory analysis to identify the underlying cause of the condition.
Pericardiocentesis is also used in emergency situations to remove excessive accumulations of blood or fluid from the pericardial sac, such as with cardiac tamponade. When fluid builds up too rapidly or excessively in the pericardial cavity, the resulting compression on the heart impairs the pumping action of the vascular system. Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening condition that requires immediate treatment.

Context: The removal of pericardial fluid from the sac surrounding the heart is a key procedure in diagnosing and treating conditions such as pericarditis, cardiac tamponade, and pericardial effusion. This process involves the insertion of a needle to aspirate fluid for analysis or to relieve compression on the heart due to excessive fluid accumulation.

Content: Pericardiocentesis is the removal by needle of pericardial fluid from the sac surrounding the heart for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes.

Context: The pericardium, which normally contains a small amount of fluid, can become compromised due to various factors such as infection, trauma, surgery, or disease, leading to excessive fluid accumulation in the pericardial cavity, a condition known as pericardial effusion. This chunk provides an overview of the causes of abnormal fluid buildup surrounding the heart.

Content: The pericardium, the sac (or membrane) that surrounds the heart muscle, normally contains a small amount of fluid that cushions and lubricates the heart as the heart expands and contracts. When too much fluid gathers in the pericardial cavity, the space between the pericardium and the outer layers of the heart, a condition known as pericardial effusion occurs. Abnormal amounts of fluid may result from:
- pericarditis (caused by infection, inflammation)
- trauma (producing blood in the pericardial sac)
- surgery or other invasive procedures performed on the heart
- cancer (producing malignant effusions)
- myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure
- renal failure

Context: This chunk discusses potential complications and risks associated with pericardiocentesis, an invasive procedure used to remove excess fluid from the sac surrounding the heart.

Content: Pericardiocentesis is an invasive procedure, and infection of the puncture site or pericardium is always a risk. Possible complications include perforation of a major artery, lung, or liver. The myocardium, the outer muscle layer of the heart, could also be damaged if the cardiac needle is inserted too deeply.

Context: This section describes the technical procedure of pericardiocentesis, outlining the steps taken by a physician to perform the procedure, including preparation, needle insertion, fluid aspiration, and post-procedure care.

Content: The patient's vital signs are monitored throughout the procedure, and an ECG tracing is continuously run. If time allows, sedation is administered, the puncture site is cleaned with an antiseptic iodine solution, and a local anesthetic is injected into the skin to numb the area. The patient is instructed to remain still. The physician performing pericardiocentesis will insert a syringe with an attached cardiac needle slowly into the chest wall until the needle tip reaches the pericardial sac. The patient may experience a sensation of pressure as the needle enters the membrane. When the needle is in the correct position, the physician will aspirate, or withdraw, fluid from the pericardial sac.  
When the procedure is performed for diagnostic purposes, the fluid will be collected into specimen tubes for laboratory analysis. If the pericardiocentesis is performed to treat a cardiac tamponade or other significant fluid build-up, a pericardial catheter may be attached to the needle to allow for continuous drainage.  
After the cardiac needle is removed, pressure is applied to the puncture site for approximately five minutes, and the site is then bandaged.

Context: This section provides essential information on preparing patients for pericardiocentesis, including informed consent, preparation procedures, and post-procedure care. It explains how to ensure patient safety while performing the procedure and emphasizes the importance of monitoring and managing potential complications.

Content: Prior to pericardiocentesis, the test procedure is explained to the patient, along with the risks and possible complications involved, and the patient is asked to sign an informed consent form. If the patient is incapacitated, the same steps are followed with a family member.  
No special diet or fasting is required for the test. After the patient changes into a hospital gown, an intravenous line is inserted into a vein in the arm. The IV will be used to administer sedation, and any required medications or blood products. Leads for an electrocardiogram (ECG) tracing are attached to the patient's right and left arms and legs, and the fifth lead is attached to the cardiac needle used for the procedure. The patient is instructed to lie flat on the table, with the upper body elevated to a 60 degree angle.  ## Aftercare
The site of the puncture and any drainage catheter should be checked regularly for signs of infection such as redness and swelling. Blood pressure and pulse are also monitored following the procedure. Patients who experience continued bleeding or abnormal swelling of the puncture site, sudden dizziness, difficulty breathing, or chest pains in the days following a pericardiocentesis procedure should seek immediate medical attention.

Context: To understand the importance of an echocardiogram during pericardiocentesis, consider that it's a diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of pericardial effusion and guide the needle insertion, while also reducing the risk of puncturing vital organs by identifying the correct location of the fluid accumulation. This chunk highlights the procedural steps taken to ensure accurate diagnosis and safe treatment.

Content: Whenever possible, an echocardiogram (ultrasound test) should be performed to confirm the presence of the pericardial effusion and to guide the pericardiocentesis needle during the procedure. Because of the risk of accidental puncture to major arteries or organs in pericardiocentesis, surgical drainage may be a preferred treatment option for pericardial effusion in non-emergency situations.

Context: This section provides critical information on specific scenarios and tools used in Pericardiocentesis, specifically highlighting Cardiac Tamponade, Catheters, Echocardiograms, and Electrocardiograms as essential concepts related to the procedure.

Content: Cardiac tamponade—Compression and restriction of the heart that occurs when the pericardium fills with blood or fluid. This increase in pressure outside the heart interferes with heart function and can result in shock and/or death.
Catheter—A long, thin, flexible tube used to drain or administer fluids.
Echocardiogram—An imaging test using high-frequency sound waves to obtain pictures of the heart and surrounding tissues.
Electrocardiogram—A cardiac test that measures the electrical activity of the heart.

Context: Normal pericardial fluid is characterized by its appearance and volume, which can help determine the presence and severity of pericardial effusion in patients undergoing pericardiocentesis. Understanding normal pericardial fluid parameters is crucial for diagnosing and treating conditions such as pericarditis, cardiac tamponade, and myocardial infarction.

Content: Normal pericardial fluid is clear to straw-colored in appearance with no bacteria, blood, cancer cells or pathogens. There is typically a minimal amount of the fluid (10–50 ml) in the pericardial cavity.

Context: A large volume of pericardial fluid is a key indicator of pericardial effusion, which can be caused by various conditions such as infection, trauma, or cancer. Laboratory analysis of the fluid can aid in diagnosing the underlying cause of pericarditis, and abnormal fluid characteristics can suggest specific diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus or myocardial infarction.

Content: A large volume of pericardial fluid (over 50 ml) indicates the presence of pericardial effusion. Laboratory analysis of the fluid can aid in the diagnosis of the cause of pericarditis. The presence of an infectious organism such as staphylococcus aureus is a sign of bacterial pericarditis. Excessive protein is present in cases of systemic lupus erythematosus or myocardial infarction (heart attack). An elevated white blood count may point to a fungal infection. If the patient has a hemorrhage, a cardiac rupture, or cancer, there may be blood in the pericardial fluid.

Context: This excerpt discusses two key terms relevant to pericardiocentesis: myocardium, which refers to the middle layer of the heart wall, and pericardium, a double-layered sac surrounding the heart that may accumulate fluid. This information is crucial in understanding the location and condition of the pericardial cavity where the procedure occurs.

Content: Myocardium—The middle layer of the heart wall. Pericardium—A double membranous sac that envelops and protects the heart.

Context: This passage provides an overview of pericarditis, including its prevalence, common causes (viral infections), demographic risk factors, and recurrence rates. It sets the stage for further discussion on the various forms of pericarditis and their underlying causes.

Content: Pericarditis is fairly common. It affects approximately one in 1,000 people. The most common form is caused by infection with a virus. People in their 20s and 30s who have had a recent upper respiratory infection are most likely to be affected, along with men aged 20–50. One out of every four people who have had pericarditis will get it again, but after two years these relapses are less likely.

Context: Pericarditis is an inflammation of the pericardium, a thin membrane surrounding the heart. It can be caused by various factors, including viral infections, injury to the heart, or inflammatory diseases. This condition affects approximately 1 in 1,000 people worldwide, with men and those in their 20s-30s being more susceptible.

Content: Pericarditis is an inflammation of the two layers of the thin, sac-like membrane that surrounds the heart. This membrane is called the pericardium, so the term pericarditis means inflammation of the pericardium.

Context: This section discusses the common causes of pericarditis, including viral infections, inflammatory diseases, bacteria, fungi, parasites, and other conditions that can lead to the inflammation of the pericardium. It provides a general overview of the various factors that contribute to the development of pericarditis.

Content: The viruses that cause pericarditis include those that cause influenza, polio, and rubella (German measles). In children, the most common viruses that cause pericarditis are the adenovirus and the cocksackievirus (which is most likely to affect children during warmer weather).  
Although pericarditis is usually caused by a virus, it also can be caused by an injury to the heart or it can follow a heart attack. It may also be caused by certain inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or systemic lupus erythematosus. Bacteria, fungi, parasites, tuberculosis, cancer or kidney failure may also affect the pericardium. Sometimes the cause is unknown.  
There are several forms of pericarditis, depending on the cause.

Context: This part explains the specific type of pericarditis caused by infections, including viruses, bacteria, or fungi, describing its symptoms and terminology related to bacterial pericarditis.

Content: This is caused by infection with a virus, bacteria, or fungus—usually in the lungs and upper respiratory tract. This form of the disease causes a sharp, severe pain that starts in the region of the breastbone. If the pericarditis is caused by a bacteria, it is called bacterial or purulent pericarditis.

Context: Symptoms of Constrictive Pericarditis Include: Rapid Breathing, Breathlessness.

Content: Symptoms likely to be associated with pericarditis include:
- rapid breathing
- breathlessness

Context: This chunk discusses the underlying cause of constrictive pericarditis, specifically how the pericardium's scarring or thickening hinders heart contraction due to tuberculosis or other factors.

Content: When the pericardium is scarred or thickened, the heart has difficulty contracting. This is because the pericardium has shrunken or tightened around the heart, constricting the muscle's heart movement. This usually occurs as a result of tuberculosis, which now is rarely found in the United States, except in immigrant, AIDS, and prison populations.

Context: This section explains how pericardial effusion, a condition where fluid accumulates between the heart and pericardium, can lead to cardiac tamponade, highlighting its causes, consequences, and importance as a serious medical emergency requiring immediate treatment.

Content: Sometimes fluid collects between the heart and the pericardium. This is called pericardial effusion, and may lead to a condition called cardiac tamponade. When the fluid accumulates, it can squeeze the heart and prevent it from filling with blood. This keeps the rest of the body from getting the necessary supply of oxygen and can cause dangerously low blood pressure. A cardiac tamponade can happen when the chest is injured during surgery, radiation therapy, or an accident. Cardiac tamponade is a serious medical emergency and must be treated immediately.

Context: Symptoms associated with Constrictive Pericarditis, a condition where the heart has difficulty contracting due to scarred or thickened pericardium, can include respiratory distress (rapid breathing, dry cough), pain in the chest and neck, fever, chills, weakness, anxiety, and swelling of neck veins.

Content: - dry cough
- fever and chills
- weakness
- broken blood vessels (hemorrhages) in the mucus membrane of the eyes, the back, the chest, fingers, and toes
- feelings of anxiety
- A sharp or dull pain that starts in the front of the chest under the breastbone and radiates to the left side of the neck, upper abdomen, and left shoulder the pain is less intense when the patient sits up or leans forward and worsens when lying down; it may worsen with a deep breath, like pleurisy, which may accompany pericarditis
In cardiac tamponade, neck veins may be swollen and blood pressure may be very low.

Context: A person with constrictive pericarditis may experience symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, and dry cough. The condition is characterized by a stiffened pericardium surrounding the heart, leading to impaired heart function and difficulty in contracting the muscle's heart movement.

Content: The heart of a person with pericarditis is likely to produce a grating sound (friction rub) when heard through a stethoscope. This sound occurs because the roughened pericardium surfaces are rubbing against each other.
The following tests will also help diagnose pericarditis and what is causing it:
- electrocardiograph (ECG) and echocardiogram to distinguish between pericarditis and a heart attack.

Context: In the diagnosis and treatment of constrictive pericarditis, imaging tests such as X-rays, CT scans, heart catheterization, and blood tests help to identify fluid build-up, cardiac chambers and valves, potential infections or cancers, and cardiac enzymes.

Content: - x ray to show the traditional ''water bottle'' shadow around the heart that is often seen in pericarditis where there is a sufficient fluid build up.
- computed tomography scan (CT scan) of the chest.
- heart catheterization to view the heart's chambers and valves.
- pericardiocentesisto test for viruses, bacteria, fungus, cancer, and tuberculosis.
- blood tests such as LDH and CPK to measure cardiac enzymes and distinguish between a heart attack and pericarditis, as well as a complete blood count (CBC) to look for infection.

Context: This chunk discusses the treatment and management of pericarditis, specifically highlighting that most cases are caused by a virus and will heal naturally without specific curative treatment. It explains the use of various medications to reduce inflammation and describes potential interventions for recurrence or complications such as constrictive pericarditis.

Content: Since most pericarditis is caused by a virus and will heal naturally, there is no specific, curative treatment. Ordinary antibiotics do not work against viruses. Pericarditis that comes from a virus usually clears up in two weeks to three months. Medications may be used to reduce inflammation, however. They include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen and aspirin. Corticosteroids are helpful if the pericarditis was caused by a heart attack orsystemic lupus erythematosus. Analgesics (painkillers such as aspirin or acetaminophen) also may be given.  
If the pericarditis recurs, removal of all or part of the pericardium (pericardiectomy) may be necessary. In the case of constrictive pericarditis, the pericardiectomy may be necessary to remove the stiffened  If a cardiac tamponade is present, it may be necessary to drain excess fluid from the pericardium. Pericardiocentesis, the same procedure used for testing, will be used to withdraw the fluid.  
For most people, home care with rest and medications to relieve pain are sufficient. A warm heating pad or compress also may help relieve pain. Sitting in an upright position and bending forward helps relieve discomfort. A person with pericarditis may also be kept in bed, with the head of the bed elevated to reduce the heart's need to work hard as it pumps blood. Along with painkillers and antibiotics, diuretic drugs (''water pills'') to reduce fluids may also be used judiciously.

Context: This statement is part of the general information section discussing prevention and general health advice for individuals diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis, highlighting the importance of maintaining a healthy lifestyle to boost immune function.

Content: There is no way to prevent pericarditis, but a healthy lifestyle with proper nutrition and exercise will help keep the body's immune system strong and more likely to fight off invading microorganisms.

Context: This statement provides hope for patients diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis, a condition where the heart's ability to pump blood is severely impaired due to scarring or thickening of the surrounding membrane. Recovery within several months without additional treatment offers a positive outlook for many individuals affected by this rare but serious medical condition.

Content: Prognosis is good. Most people recover within three weeks to several months and do not need any additional treatment.

Context: This section explains medical procedures used to diagnose and treat constrictive pericarditis, including heart catheterization to visualize the heart's chambers and valves, pericardiocentesis to test for infections, and a description of the pericardium, which plays a key role in the condition.

Content: Heart catheterization—A heart catheterization is used to view the heart's chamber and valves. A tube (catheter) is inserted into an artery, usually in the groin. A dye is then put into the artery through the tube. The dye makes its way to the heart to create an image of the heart on x-ray film. The image is photographed and stored for further examination.
Pericardiocentesis—Pericardiocentesis is a procedure used to test for viruses, bacteria, and fungus. The physician puts a small tube through the skin, directly into the pericardial sac, and withdraws fluid. The fluid then is tested for viruses, bacteria, and fungus.
Pericardium—The pericardium is the thin, sac-like membrane that surrounds the heart. It has two layers: the serous pericardium and the fibrous pericardium. parts of the pericardium that are preventing the heart from beating correctly.

Context: This section describes various diagnostic tests used to diagnose and understand constrictive pericarditis, including Computed Tomography (CT) scan, Echocardiogram, Electrocardiogram (ECG), and others. These tests help doctors visualize the heart's structure, assess fluid buildup, and measure electrical activity to confirm the diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis.

Content: Computed tomography (CT) scan—A CT scan uses x rays to scan the body from many angles. A computer compiles the x rays into a picture of the area being studied. The images are viewed on a monitor and printed-out.
Echocardiogram—An echocardiogram bounces sound waves off the heart to create a picture of its chambers and valves.
Electrocardiogram (ECG)—An ECG is a test to measure electrical activity in the heart.

Context: This text provides an overview of perinatal infections, explaining how they can be transmitted from mother to baby during pregnancy or delivery, their potential complications, and the importance of seeking medical treatment for both mothers and sexual partners. It sets the stage for discussing specific bacterial and viral illnesses that can cause these infections.

Content: Perinatal infections include bacterial or viral illnesses that can be passed from a mother to her baby either while the baby is still in the uterus, during the delivery process, or shortly after birth. Maternal infection can, in some cases, cause complications at birth. The mother may or may not experience active symptoms of the infection during the pregnancy. The most serious and most common perinatal infections, and the impact of these diseases on the mother and infant, are discussed below in alphabetical order. It is important to note that men can become infected and can transmit many of these infections to other women. The sexual partners of women who have these infections also should seek medical treatment.

Context: This chunk provides an introductory definition of perinatal infections, highlighting their potential transmission from mother to baby during pregnancy or delivery. It sets the stage for discussions on specific bacterial and viral infections that can cause these transmissions, such as chlamydia trachomatis, cytomegalovirus, genital herpes, hepatitis B, human immunodeficiency virus, and human papillomavirus.

Content: An infection caused by a bacteria or virus that can be passed from a mother to her baby during pregnancy or delivery is called a perinatal infection.

Context: This section explains how certain viruses, specifically Cytomegalovirus (CMV), can be transmitted from mother to infant during pregnancy or delivery, highlighting its potential impact on fetal development and birth outcomes.

Content: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common virus in the herpes virus family. It is found in saliva, urine, and other body fluids and can be spread through sexual contact or other more casual forms of physical contact like kissing. In adults, CMV may cause mild symptoms of swollen lymph glands, fever, and fatigue. Many people who carry the virus experience no symptoms at all. Infants can become infected with CMV while still in the uterus if the mother becomes infected or develops a recurrence of the infection during pregnancy. Most infants exposed to CMV before birth develop normally and do not show any symptoms. As many as 6,000 infants who were exposed to CMV before birth are born with serious complications each year. CMV interferes with normal fetal development and can cause mental retardation, blindness, deafness, or epilepsy in these infants.

Context: This chunk describes Chlamydia trachomatis, a bacterial sexually transmitted disease that can cause serious complications in newborns during delivery, including eye infections and pneumonia. It discusses the risks and symptoms associated with this infection, providing essential information for pregnant women and healthcare providers.

Content: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted disease in the United States, causing more than 4 million infections each year. The majority of women with chlamydial infection experience no obvious symptoms. The infection affects the reproductive tract and causes pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy (the fertilized egg implants somewhere other than in the uterus). This infection can cause premature rupture of the membranes and early labor. It can be passed to the infant during delivery and can cause ophthalmia neonatorum (an eye infection) within the first month of life and pneumonia within one to three months of age. Symptoms of chlamydial pneumonia are a repetitive cough and rapid breathing. Wheezing is rare and the infant does not develop a fever.

Context: This section discusses the risks of genital herpes transmission from mother to infant during delivery, highlighting its potential complications, including miscarriage, low birth weight, and severe neurological conditions like HSV-2 encephalitis. It emphasizes the importance of prompt medical attention for women with active genital herpes sores during pregnancy.

Content: Genital herpes, which is usually caused by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), is a sexually transmitted disease that causes painful sores on the genitals. Women who have their first outbreak of genital herpes during pregnancy are at high risk of miscarriage or delivering a low birth weight baby. The infection can be passed to the infant at the time of delivery if the mother has an active sore. The most serious risk to the infant is the possibility of developing HSV-2 encephalitis, an inflammation of the brain, with symptoms of irritability and poor feeding.

Context: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is one of several serious perinatal infections that can be passed from a mother to her baby during pregnancy or delivery, causing acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). This section discusses the risk of HIV transmission and its devastating impact on infant health.

Content: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a serious, contagious virus that causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). About one-fourth of pregnant women with HIV pass the infection on to their newborn infants. An infant with HIV usually develops AIDS and dies before the age of two.

Context: Hepatitis B is a contagious virus that can be transmitted from mother to infant during delivery, posing a significant risk to newborns born to mothers testing positive for the hepatitis B virus. This highlights one of the perinatal infections discussed in this document, which emphasizes the importance of prenatal care and blood screening to prevent transmission.

Content: Hepatitis B is a contagious virus that causes liver damage and is a leading cause of chronic liver disease and cirrhosis. Approximately 20,000 infants are born each year to mothers who test positive for the hepatitis B virus. These infants are at high risk for developing hepatitis B infection through exposure to their mothers blood during delivery.

Context: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is one of several sexually transmitted diseases that can be passed from a mother to her infant during pregnancy or delivery, posing risks to the baby's health, including development of genital warts and increased risk of cancer. This information highlights another perinatal infection risk associated with maternal HPV infection.

Content: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a sexually transmitted disease that causes genital warts and can increase the risk of developing some cancers. HPV appears to be transferred from the mother to the infant during the birth process.

Context: This information explains how rubella infection affects pregnant women and their developing infants, including serious birth defects and potential consequences of transmission during pregnancy.

Content: Rubella is a virus that causes German measles, an illness that includes rash, fever, and symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection. Most people are exposed to rubella during childhood and develop antibodies to the virus so they will never get it again. Rubella infection during early pregnancy can pass through the placenta to the developing infant and cause serious birth defects including heart abnormalities, mental retardation, blindness, and deafness.

Context: This section discusses Group B streptococcus (GBS), a common bacterial cause of infection and death in newborn infants, which shares some similarities with the risks associated with rubella, particularly regarding birth defects and neonatal infections.

Content: Group B streptococcus (GBS) infection is the most common bacterial cause of infection and death in newborn infants. Although rates have declined in the United States since the introduction of antibiotics to at-risk women during labor in the 1980s, about 1,600 cases and 80 newborn deaths still occur each year. In women, GBS can cause vaginitis and urinary tract infections. Both infections can cause premature birth and the bacteria can be transferred to the infant in the uterus or during delivery. GBS causes pneumonia, meningitis, and other serious infections in infants.

Context: This excerpt describes the risks associated with syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection that can be passed from mother to child during pregnancy, potentially leading to birth defects or infant mortality. The information is presented in the context of prenatal care and potential complications related to rubella (German measles) transmission.

Content: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection that can be transferred from a mother to an infant through the placenta before birth. Up to 50% of infants born to mothers with syphilis will be premature, stillborn, or will die shortly after birth. Infected infants may have severe birth defects. Those infants who survive infancy may develop symptoms of syphilis up to two years later.

Context: Chlamydial infections are sexually transmitted and can be diagnosed during pregnancy, posing risks such as premature birth and bacterial transmission to newborns. This information is relevant to prenatal care and prevention strategies for pregnant women, highlighting an additional concern beyond rubella and other common birth defects and infections associated with pregnancy.

Content: Chlamydial bacteria can be diagnosed by taking a cotton swab sample of the cervix and vagina during the third trimester of the pregnancy. Chlamydial cell cultures take three to seven days to grow but many laboratories are not equipped to run the tests necessary to confirm the diagnosis.

Context: This information provides an overview of common maternal infections that can impact pregnancy, including CMV. It is situated alongside other sections on syphilis, herpes simplex virus-2 (HSV-2), hepatitis B, and group B streptococcus, which also discuss potential risks to pregnant women and their newborns.

Content: Past or recent infection with CMV can be identified by antibody tests and CMV can be grown from body fluids.

Context: This instruction pertains to prenatal testing for hepatitis B during pregnancy, which is mentioned in the section discussing various infections that pregnant women can be tested for, such as syphilis, HIV, HPV, and rubella.

Content: A blood test can be used to screen pregnant women for the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in prenatal health programs.

Context: This statement is part of a section discussing sexually transmitted infections, including syphilis, chlamydia, CMV, and genital herpes, in relation to pregnancy and newborns. It highlights the importance of testing and treatment for these conditions during pregnancy and after birth, as they can pose significant risks to maternal and infant health.

Content: The appearance of a genital sore is enough to suspect an outbreak of genital herpes. The sore can be cultured and tested to confirm that HSV-2 is present.

Context: Testing for rubella antibodies is part of prenatal screening to determine if a pregnant woman has previously been infected, reducing the risk of transmission during pregnancy, which can lead to serious birth defects in infants.

Content: Pregnant women are usually tested for antibodies to rubella, which would indicate that they have been previously exposed to the virus and therefore would not develop infection during pregnancy if exposed.

Context: HIV is discussed alongside other STIs, but its relevance to rubella (German measles) is not explicitly mentioned. However, some medical literature suggests that HIV-positive individuals can pass on their infection to others through bodily fluids during pregnancy or childbirth, potentially posing a risk to the infant. This mention of HIV serves as an introduction to discussing prenatal screening programs and infectious disease transmission.

Content: HIV can be detected using a blood test and is part of most prenatal screening programs.

Context: This information is about the detection methods for Group B streptococcus (GBS), a common bacterial cause of infection and death in newborn infants, which is distinct from rubella (German measles) but often co-occurs during pregnancy.

Content: GBS can be detected by a vaginal or rectal swab culture, and sometimes from a urine culture. Blood tests can be used to confirm GBS infection in infants who exhibit symptoms.

Context: This information is part of a medical document discussing various viral infections, including rubella. It specifically addresses sexually transmitted infections such as Human Papillomavirus (HPV) in relation to genital herpes and warts, distinguishing it from other topics like GBS, syphilis, chlamydia, CMV, HSV-2, hepatitis B, and HIV within the broader context of prenatal care and pregnancy.

Content: HPV causes the growth of warts in the genital area. The wart tissue can be removed with a scalpel and tested to determine what type of HPV virus caused the infection.

Context: This text discusses treatment options for pregnant women infected with rubella during the third trimester, including oral erythromycin and its effects on newborn infants, as part of managing complications associated with German measles.

Content: Pregnant women can be treated during the third trimester with oral erythromycin, for seven–14 days depending on the dose used. Newborn infants can be treated with erythromycin liquid for 10–14 days at a dosage determined by their body weight.

Context: This section discusses prenatal testing for syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection that can be passed from mother to child during pregnancy. It provides information on symptoms, diagnosis methods, treatment options, and preventative measures to protect both mother and infant from its potential complications.

Content: Pregnant women are usually tested for syphilis as part of the prenatal screening.

Context: This section discusses congenital infections, specifically CMV, which is not directly related to Rubella. It provides information on diagnosis, treatment, and prevention options for CMV, highlighting its distinction from other maternal and neonatal infections like GBS and syphilis mentioned earlier in the document.

Content: No drugs or vaccines are currently available for prevention or treatment of CMV.

Context: "Managing HIV in pregnant women, including prenatal care, testing, treatment, and drug therapy to prevent perinatal transmission and infant development of AIDS."

Content: Recent studies have shown that prenatal care and HIV testing before delivery are major opportunities to prevent perinatal HIV infection. Pregnant women with HIV should be treated as early in the pregnancy as possible with zidovudine (AZT). Other newer drugs designed to treat HIV/AIDS also may be used during pregnancy with the knowledge that these drugs may have unknown effects on the infant. The risks and benefits of such treatments need to be discussed. Infants born with HIV should receive aggressive drug treatment to prevent development of AIDS.

Context: Infants born to mothers who test positive to the HBsAg test are at risk for hepatitis B infection, but this information is not related to rubella or German measles.

Content: Infants born to mothers who test positive to the HBsAg test should be treated with hepatitis B immune globulin at birth to give them immediate protection against developing hepatitis B. These infants, as well as all infants, should also receive a series of three hepatitis B vaccine injections as part of their routine immunizations.

Context: This text discusses treatments and prevention measures for various infections that can affect pregnant women or their newborns, including rubella, which is also mentioned in relation to potential complications during pregnancy. It covers antiviral medication for suspected herpes simplex virus (HSV-2), hepatitis B infection, and CMV, as well as delivery recommendations for mothers with active cases of genital herpes.

Content: The antiviral drugs acyclovir or famciclovir can be administered to the mother during pregnancy. Little is known about the risks of these drugs to the fetus, however, the risk of birth defects does not seem to be any higher than for women who do not take these medications. Infants with suspected HSV-2 can be treated with acyclovir. Delivery of the infant by cesarean section is recommended if the mother has an active case of genital herpes.

Context: This section discusses genital warts, a common sexually transmitted infection, in relation to pregnancy and childbirth, drawing parallels with HIV transmission risks and prevention methods.

Content: Genital warts are very difficult to treat and frequently recur even after treatment. They can be removed by cryotherapy (freezing), laser or electrocauterization (burning), or surgical excision (cutting) of the warts. Some medications (imiquimod 5% cream, podophyllin, trichloroacetic acid or topical 5-fluorouracil) can be applied to help dissolve genital warts. Cesarean delivery rather than vaginal delivery seems to reduce the risk of transmission of HPV from mothers to infants.

Context: This section discusses prenatal care, rubella exposure, and pregnancy complications, providing general information on potential risks and consequences during pregnancy, unrelated to specific HIV treatments or prevention methods.

Content: No treatment is available. Some health care providers may recommend giving the mother an injection of immune globulin (to boost the immune system to fight off the virus) if she is exposed to rubella early in the pregnancy. However, no evidence to support the use of these injections exists. Exposure to rubella early in pregnancy poses a high risk that the infant will have serious birth defects. Termination of the pregnancy may be considered. Women who have not been previously exposed to rubella will usually be vaccinated immediately after the first pregnancy to protect infants of future pregnancies.

Context: This section discusses prevention and treatment measures for Group B Streptococcus (GBS) infection during pregnancy, which is a separate topic from HIV, although both conditions require prenatal care and preventive measures to protect the mother and newborn.

Content: Pregnant women diagnosed with GBS late in the pregnancy should be treated with antibiotics injected intravenously to prevent premature labor. In 2003, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued revised guidelines for preventing perinatal GBS disease. They began recommending that women not only be tested as soon as they learn of their pregnancy, but again at 35 to 37 weeks gestation. The CDC also recommended updated prophylaxis regimens for women with penicillin allergies, as well as new guidelines for patients with threatened preterm deliveries and other new recommendations. If transmission of GBS to the newborn infant already is suspected or if the baby develops symptoms of infection, infants often are treated with antibiotics.

Context: Antibiotic therapy is sometimes used in pregnancy to treat various infections, including those that can be transmitted to infants. In the context of HIV prevention, early antibiotic treatment may help prevent transmission from mother to infant, although no evidence supports the use of antibiotics specifically for HIV prevention.

Content: Antibiotic therapy, usually penicillin, given early in the pregnancy can be used to treat the infection and may prevent transmission to the infant.

Context: This chunk discusses complications associated with chlamydial infection, specifically premature delivery, which is unrelated to HIV. However, it mentions that treatment with antibiotics during pregnancy can prevent transmission to the baby, implying a connection to prenatal care practices that may be relevant to HIV-infected mothers.

Content: Without treatment, the most serious consequences of chlamydial infection are related to complications of premature delivery. Treatment of the mother with antibiotics during the third trimester can prevent premature delivery and the transfer of the infection to the baby. Infants treated with antibiotics for eye infection or pneumonia generally recover.

Context: This chunk provides definitions related to pregnancy, childbirth, and medical complications, such as cesarean section, ectopic pregnancy, encephalitis, and perinatal, which are separate from HIV treatment and management.

Content: Cesarean section—A surgical procedure in which an incision is made in a woman's abdomen to deliver the infant from the uterus.
Ectopic pregnancy—A condition that ends in miscarriage, in which the fertilized ovum attaches somewhere other than in the uterus (for example in the fallopian tube or abdomen).
Encephalitis—Inflammation or swelling of the brain.
Perinatal—The period of time around the time of pregnancy and delivery.

Context: Pneumonia is not mentioned in relation to HIV, but rather as a general medical condition. This definition provides information on pneumonia that does not fit within the rest of the document's focus on HIV-related topics.

Content: Pneumonia—An infection and inflammation of the lungs that usually causes shortness of breath, cough, fever, and chest pain.

Context: This chunk discusses the potential severity of Cytomegalovirus (CMV) exposure, particularly in vulnerable populations such as those with compromised immune systems, highlighting the risk of serious complications, birth defects, and lifelong consequences for both mothers and infants.

Content: The chance for recovery after exposure to CMV is very good for both the mother and the infant. Exposure to CMV can be serious and even life threatening for mothers and infants whose immune systems are compromised, for example those receiving chemotherapy or who have HIV/AIDS. Those infants who develop birth defects after CMV exposure may have serious, lifelong complications.

Context: This section discusses preventive measures against hepatitis B infection, which is unrelated to Cytomegalovirus (CMV), a common viral infection that can affect both mother and infant during pregnancy.

Content: Infants treated at birth with immune globulin and the series of vaccinations will be protected from development of hepatitis B infection. Infants infected with hepatitis B develop a chronic, mild form of hepatitis and are at increased risk for developing liver disease.

Context: This statement discusses the potential long-term effects of Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, specifically highlighting the recurrent nature of genital herpes sores in infected individuals, emphasizing the need for ongoing vigilance during their lifetimes.

Content: Once a woman or infant is infected, outbreaks of genital herpes sores can recur at any point during their lifetimes.

Context: This statement is part of a general discussion about preventable infections that can affect pregnant women, their infants, and newborns, emphasizing the importance of prenatal care and preventive measures to mitigate risks associated with various infectious diseases.

Content: Treatment with AZT during pregnancy significantly reduces the chance that the infant will be infected with HIV from the mother.

Context: This text mentions an increased risk of premature birth, birth defects, or serious syphilis symptoms in untreated pregnant women, highlighting a potential consequence of infections unrelated to CMV.
